subject: mangrove rivulus fish
title: A Fish That Lives Inside Rotting Logs for 66 Days Without Water

scenes.text: Scientists split open a rotting log in a swamp. Fish fell out.
The mangrove rivulus is a five-centimeter killifish from the swamps of Florida, Belize and Brazil.
When its pools dry up, it crawls into crab burrows, leaf piles, coconuts, old beer cans, and the tunnels insects chew through logs.
In the lab, these fish survived 66 days out of water without eating. How? They breathe through their skin.
The skin is paper-thin and packed with blood vessels, so it takes in oxygen and dumps waste, the job gills normally do.
And it is the only vertebrate that fertilizes its own eggs, so one fish in one log can start a clone colony. Open the next log carefully.

description:
The mangrove rivulus, a killifish about 5 cm long from the mangrove swamps of Florida, Belize and Brazil, can live out of water for up to 66 days in laboratory tests, without eating. When pools dry up it hides in crab burrows, damp leaf litter, coconuts, discarded cans and the galleries insects bore through rotting logs.
Out of water it breathes through thin, capillary-rich skin, which also excretes nitrogen waste, and it plugs its gills with a mass of cells so they do not collapse. Research led by Scott Taylor and Patricia Wright was published in The American Naturalist in 2007. It is also the only vertebrate known to naturally self-fertilize, producing clones of itself.
